title: First-order definability of regular tree languages
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a finite bottom-up automaton A for finite unranked ordered labeled trees, always halts and decides whether some first-order sentence \(\varphi\) using label predicates, strict descendant and sibling order satisfies A accepts t if and only if \(t\models \varphi\) for every finite input tree t?
why: The tree analogue of effective first-order definability for regular word languages.
status_note: The 2024 primary finite-tree study explicitly retains the general first-order-definability problem. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established decision or undecidability theorem for this ordered finite-tree target. The 2025 infinite-tree and 2026 restricted temporal results are distinguished.
review_note: Specified unranked ordered finite trees, an explicit finite bottom-up table presentation and the exact first-order vocabulary. Matched sibling order plus descendant to the source’s lexicographic signature. Checked the source and subsequent primary statements without independently auditing their proofs.

progress.text: An effective characterization is proved for \(\Delta _{2}\) over finite ordered trees, including the ancestor-plus-lexicographic signature.
New effective necessary and sufficient tests in a finite-tree algebra setting remain separate rather than forming a full criterion.
A first-order automata characterization is obtained for unordered infinite trees, a different semantic domain.
A temporal-logic common-fragment decision theorem does not decide unrestricted FO-definability on finite ordered trees.

sentences: Can one decide whether a regular language of finite ordered trees has a first-order definition?
The automaton is finite input, while the sought sentence must describe its language on trees of every finite size.
The logic can inspect labels, descendants and sibling order but cannot quantify over sets of nodes.
Known fragment tests and separate necessary or sufficient algebraic conditions leave the full decision problem unresolved.
Recent infinite-tree and restricted temporal-logic characterizations do not establish this finite ordered-tree test.

upgraded_from.title: First-order definability of regular tree languages

definitions: A tree is a finite nonempty set T of finite words over positive integers, containing the empty word \(\varepsilon\), closed under prefixes, and such that \(ui\in T\) implies \(uj\in T\) for \(1\le j\le i\). Its root is \(\varepsilon\); the children of u are \(u1,\ldots ,uk\) in that order. Each node has exactly one label from a nonempty finite alphabet \(\Sigma\). There is no fixed bound on k. \(Desc(x,y)\) means x is a proper prefix of y, so y is a strict descendant of x. \(Sib(x,y)\) means \(x=ui\) and \(y=uj\) for the same parent u with \(i<j\); it orders siblings, not all incomparable nodes. Equality and the unary predicates \(\mathrm{P}_{a}(x)\), one per label \(a\in \Sigma\), complete the logical vocabulary. First-order sentences are finite formulas formed from these atomic predicates by Boolean connectives and quantification over individual nodes only, with any finite number of variables and alternations. No quantification over sets, counting quantifier or extra transitive-closure operator is allowed. The parent relation is definable from Desc. The lexicographic order used in the primary paper is equivalent to Desc plus Sib: x precedes y if \(Desc(x,y)\), or some sibling s of t precedes it with s equal to or an ancestor of x and t equal to or an ancestor of y. Conversely Sib is definable from parent and lexicographic order. To fix a finite input presentation, a bottom-up automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a binary operation ⊕ and identity 0 making \((Q,\oplus ,0) a\) monoid, a table \(\delta _{a}:Q\to Q\) for each \(a\in \Sigma\), and an accepting subset \(F\subseteq Q\). A node labeled a with ordered child states \(q_{1},\ldots ,q_{k}\) receives state \(\delta _{a}(q_{1}\oplus \cdots \oplus q_{k})\); the empty sum is 0. The tree is accepted when its root state lies in F. These finite tables, alphabet and state indices are explicitly encoded in binary; this is an algebraic bottom-up presentation of regular unranked tree languages. The algorithm must work for every valid finite presentation, without a complexity bound beyond termination. The sentence \(\varphi\) may depend on A, but must be a single sentence for all finite trees and all their sizes.
answer_criterion: Prove decidability by an algorithm that terminates correctly on every valid automaton description, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Recognizing trees with a fixed supplied automaton, deciding whether one supplied sentence agrees with an automaton, or testing definability in a fixed quantifier fragment does not decide existence of an arbitrary first-order definition.

context_blocks.title: Two descriptions of a tree property
context_blocks.text: An automaton combines finitely many states from the children and passes one state to their parent. A first-order sentence instead describes relationships between named nodes. For instance, “every a-labeled node has a b-labeled descendant” is the sentence \(\forall x\)(\(\mathrm{P}_{a}(x)\Rightarrow \exists y\)(\(Desc(x,y)\land \mathrm{P}_{b}(y)\))). The question asks whether the entire language recognized by a given automaton has some description of this logical kind.

context_blocks.title: Regular does not automatically mean first-order
context_blocks.text: A two-state bottom-up computation can track whether the total number of nodes is even or odd: combine child parities and then count the parent. First-order logic with order cannot express arbitrary parity even on trees that are single paths. Thus finite-state recognition is strictly more expressive. The task is to tell, from an automaton’s finite description, on which side of that expressiveness boundary its language lies.

context_blocks.title: The available relations change the problem
context_blocks.text: A descendant relation permits a sentence to refer directly to nodes arbitrarily far below another node. A child relation concerns just one edge. Decidability results for the child-only vocabulary therefore do not settle this card. Order among siblings is also part of the input structure: permuting subtrees can change the truth of a formula. The chosen vocabulary matches the ordered ancestor-plus-lexicographic setting of the source rather than an unordered or purely local variant.

context_blocks.title: What partial characterizations establish
context_blocks.text: Bojańczyk and Segoufin decide definability in \(\Delta _{2}\), the languages having both an existential-then-universal and a universal-then-existential definition. They do not decide arbitrary first-order definability. Blumensath’s 2024 finite-tree work supplies decidable necessary and sufficient conditions separately, but no one condition that is both. A necessary condition can fail to reject every nondefinable language, while a sufficient condition can fail to accept every definable language. The remaining gap is a complete test.

context_blocks.title: Later results concern other targets
context_blocks.text: The 2025 automata characterization studies first-order logic over unordered infinite trees. The August 2026 result decides a common fragment of particular branching-time and linear-time temporal logics. Their domains or logical restrictions differ from the full finite ordered-tree question. They do not supply the all-input terminating test requested here. A solution would turn an expressiveness boundary into a mechanically checkable property of finite-state tree specifications.
